blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The mean deviation (MD), or mean absolute deviation, is the average absolute distance of the values from a chosen centre, usually the mean: MD = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n. It can also be taken about the median: MD = Σ|x − median| ÷ n.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The range and IQR use only a couple of positions in the sorted data. The MD is the first measure here to use every value. Raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero (recall §2.2.1), so the MD drops their signs and averages the distances.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html: About which centre c is Σ|x − c| smallest? Sort the data and move c a small step δ to the right. Every value above c gets δ closer; every value below c gets δ farther. The total changes by (number below − number above) × δ. While more than half the values lie above c, moving right reduces the total; once more than half lie below, moving right increases it. The total is therefore smallest where the counts balance, at the median. So the MD about the median is never larger than the MD about the mean, or about any other point.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Five children, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 kg, mean 11. Absolute deviations: 2, 1, 0, 1, 2. MD = 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 kg: on average a child’s weight lies 1.2 kg from the mean. Here mean = median, so the MD about the median is also 1.2 kg.

Replace the 9 kg child with a 2 kg child: 2, 10, 11, 12, 13 (mean 9.6, median 11).

  • About the mean: |2 − 9.6| + |10 − 9.6| + … = 7.6 + 0.4 + 1.4 + 2.4 + 3.4 = 15.2; MD = 3.04 kg.
  • About the median: 9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 13; MD = 2.6 kg, the smaller, as the derivation promised.

For today’s 30 children the MD is 1.41 kg about either the mean or the median, because the two centres almost coincide (11.81 and 11.7 kg).

points.html: MD = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n (about the mean) or Σ|x − median| ÷ n (about the median). The MD about the median is the minimum possible.

It uses every value and is easy to explain. Its weakness is algebraic: absolute distances do not split cleanly into parts. Squared distances do (the identity in §3.6), which is why variance, not MD, became the base of later methods.
